title: Google Review Card Placement Guide
summary: A placement playbook for Google review cards that maps format choice to the real customer moment — front desk, checkout counter, tabletop prompt, pickup counter, in-room surface — and runs a two-location pilot before scaling prompts everywhere.
heroPoints: Placement decides response rate before artwork or chip choice does — a great card in the wrong moment underperforms a mediocre card in the right moment.
Front desks, checkout counters, tabletops and pickup zones each behave differently and deserve their own format choice rather than a single universal card.
The best first rollout tests one or two live placements against a written conversion target, not every possible surface at once.

sections.title: Why placement dominates the conversion math
sections.intro: Operators usually think of a review card programme as a design decision, then a print decision, then a rollout decision. In practice, placement does most of the conversion lifting — often 3–5× the effect of swapping card material or copy.
bullets: A customer gives a review when three things line up: they are satisfied, they have a free hand, and they are paused for a moment without pressure. Placement is the only lever that controls all three at once.
A premium card in a bad moment (the tabletop at a packed brunch service) converts worse than a plain sticker in a good moment (the hotel checkout while waiting for the card machine).
Placement failures look like product failures. Operators blame the card format when the real problem is that the prompt sits three steps away from the customer's natural pause.

sections.title: The five high-value placement moments
sections.intro: Across hospitality, retail and service businesses, five placement moments drive the majority of review-card conversions. Knowing which one fits the business is the first decision.
bullets: Checkout counter / front desk: the handoff moment. Card is best introduced verbally by the cashier or front-desk clerk when the transaction has just settled — 'we'd love a quick Google review if that was a good visit'. Handed over as a physical card.
Tabletop prompt: the seated moment. Card or stand lives on the table. Works in coffee shops, casual restaurants, and waiting rooms. Weaker in fine dining where the tabletop is already curated.
Pickup counter / to-go window: the short-dwell moment. Customer is waiting briefly for an order. A small stand or sticker at eye level is more effective than a card they have to take.
In-room surface: the private moment. Hotel desk, spa treatment room, fitting room. Works when the customer has time and privacy; fails when the room has no clear call to action.
Bag-drop or delivery insert: the post-purchase moment. Card rides home with the order. Effective for e-commerce and delivery; requires a separate design because the moment is not live.

sections.title: Matching format to moment
sections.intro: Each placement moment suits a specific card or prompt format. Mismatching format to moment is the single most common source of underperformance.
bullets: Handoff moment → physical NFC card, handed over by staff. Substrate and finish matter because the customer holds the card for 5–10 seconds. Premium PVC, wood or metal.
Seated moment → NFC stand or printed table tent. The prompt stays put; durability is more important than premium feel. Acrylic stand with an NFC insert is the workhorse here.
Short-dwell moment → NFC sticker or small wall-mounted prompt at eye level. Sticker on the counter edge or a 10×10 cm framed card above the pickup window.
Private moment → NFC insert in in-room collateral, or a dedicated stand on the desk. Hotel in-room desk pads with an embedded NFC chip are effective.
Post-purchase moment → printed card insert in the order. QR-first design, because the customer is no longer with a device obviously in hand. NFC as secondary.
Staff-delivered moments are about the card's hold-in-hand feel; fixed-surface moments are about legibility and durability at a glance.

sections.title: Surface and environment constraints
sections.intro: Placements fail when they ignore the physical reality of the surface. A great moment on a bad surface still underperforms.
bullets: Metal counters detune NFC antennas. If the card or stand sits on steel or aluminium, use on-metal NFC labels or raise the card off the metal with a spacer.
Glass tables reflect and scatter light, reducing QR scan reliability. Matte QR codes on reverse-contrast backgrounds outperform gloss on these surfaces.
Outdoor patios add UV exposure, rain risk, and temperature swings. Specify UV-resistant inks and waterproof substrates; replacement cadence will still be 2–3× indoor.
High-touch surfaces accumulate grease and sanitiser. Expect cards in these placements to need replacement every 60–90 days; budget accordingly.
Sight-line obstacles matter more than operators realise. A card on the counter hidden behind a card reader or tip jar is effectively invisible.

sections.title: Staff proximity and prompt integration
sections.intro: Placement has to align with whether staff will actively prompt or the card must work without prompting. These are different design problems.
bullets: Staff-prompted placements rely on a verbal cue during the handoff. The card is then handed over or pointed to. Conversion is high (5–15% of customers) when the prompt is sustained.
Self-serve placements rely entirely on the card's design to carry the ask. Conversion is lower (1–3%) but scales without training and works in unstaffed moments.
Mixed placements combine both — a fixed stand at the counter plus an occasional staff prompt. Conversion lands in the middle (2–6%) but is more resilient to staff churn.
Match staff reality: if the team is understaffed or the shift rotates fast, design for self-serve. Staff-prompted placements that cannot be sustained underperform fixed-surface cards.
Managerial oversight: a staff-prompted placement needs a weekly check that the prompt is still happening. Without that check, the prompt decays within four to six weeks.

sections.title: Pilot design: one or two locations, not all of them
sections.intro: A good pilot answers a conversion question. A bad pilot rolls cards out to every counter and hopes for signal. The discipline is to narrow the test.
bullets: Pick two contrasting placements. One high-confidence (the moment staff already uses for upsell) plus one hypothesis (a new moment the team wants to test). Not five.
Set a conversion target before the pilot starts. 'At least 10 new Google reviews per 1,000 transactions over four weeks' is a decision rule; 'see if it works' is not.
Instrument the URL. Unique URL tags per placement so review source can be attributed. Otherwise the pilot produces a review total and no information about which placement worked.
Run for four weeks minimum. Weekly variance (weather, staff shifts, holiday weekends) creates noise that disappears only with a few weeks of data.
Decision meeting: at week four, decide which placement earns the scale order. Do not roll out both by default; one winning placement compounds faster than two mediocre ones.
Losing placement: retire it or iterate once. Repeated failures at the same placement signal that the moment is wrong, not the card.

sections.title: Scaling and refresh rhythm after the pilot
sections.intro: A single location rollout is a sprint. A multi-location or multi-format rollout is a rhythm. Setting the refresh cadence up-front prevents decay.
bullets: Month 1: winning placement scales. Supplementary formats (stickers at pickup, inserts in bags) launch only after the main placement is proven.
Month 3: first refresh. Replace cards that have visible wear; review conversion per location and flag laggards for coaching.
Month 6: seasonality review. Some placements (patio, seasonal storefronts) need rotated cards for winter or summer; adjust artwork and placement accordingly.
Month 12: format review. Consider retiring placements that are not converting at 1%+ and reallocating to better-performing moments.
Measurement cadence: review conversion every 30 days. Per-location performance drives the coaching list; aggregate performance drives the programme decisions.
Decay signals: conversion halves, cards look scuffed, stand falls over, staff stops prompting. Any of these is a refresh trigger, not a crisis.

faq.question: What matters most in review card placement?
faq.answer: The customer moment — the point where the customer is satisfied, has a free hand and is paused without time pressure. Everything else (format, copy, substrate) amplifies or fails to amplify whatever the moment already offers. Operators who pick the right moment and an average card beat operators with a great card in the wrong moment, every time.

faq.question: Should teams test several placements at once?
faq.answer: Usually no. Two contrasting placements is the sweet spot — one high-confidence moment the team already trusts, plus one hypothesis worth testing. Testing five placements at once produces review totals without the per-placement attribution needed to make a scale decision.

faq.question: What is the right pilot length?
faq.answer: Four weeks minimum, because weekly variance (weather, staff rotations, holidays) is large enough to distort any shorter sample. Less than four weeks usually rewards whichever placement happened to get a good week.

faq.question: Does metal under the card actually break NFC?
faq.answer: Yes, enough to matter. Standard NFC antennas detune severely on steel or aluminium counters, reducing tap reliability. Use on-metal NFC labels, raise the card with a non-metallic spacer, or switch that placement to QR-first.

faq.question: What placement works best when staff cannot reliably prompt?
faq.answer: Self-serve placements with a strong fixed prompt — a pickup-counter sticker at eye level, a tabletop stand with clear copy, or an in-room surface with no competing calls to action. Conversion is lower than a staff-prompted handoff, but the placement is resilient to staff churn and understaffing.

faq.question: How often should placement cards be refreshed?
faq.answer: Every three months is the default for indoor placements; every six weeks for outdoor or high-touch surfaces; every 60 days for pickup counters that accumulate grease or sanitiser. Wear decay reduces conversion faster than most operators realise.

faq.question: What is the single biggest avoidable mistake in placement?
faq.answer: Placing the prompt where the team prefers it rather than where customers naturally pause. Operators consistently put cards near the point of sale because it is convenient for staff; customers often pause somewhere slightly different (waiting for the card machine, collecting a bag, stepping away from the counter). Match the placement to the customer's real moment, not the staff's convenience.
